slides.0.title: Terroir Comparison and Variety Profiles
slides.0.subtitle: A comparison framework for tasting and essays
slides.1.title: The Syrah terroir spectrum: among northern crus
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Côte-Rôtie
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Côte Blonde = gneiss, Côte Brune = mica schist (INAO); may include Viognier. General account: lifted aromatics, floral notes and fine tannins with a silky texture
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Hermitage
slides.1.highlights.1.content: One large hill; red Syrah (≥85% of estate plantings) and white from Marsanne/Roussanne (INAO). General account: the most structured, with the greatest ageing potential, often closed when young
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Cornas
slides.1.highlights.2.content: 100% Syrah (INAO). General account: a sheltered, heat-trapping amphitheatre, deep colour and robust tannins, rustic when young and needing time
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Comparison axes
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Compare on one set of axes: aroma (floral / black fruit / smoke), tannin texture, acidity, alcohol and ageing speed; state similarities first (all Syrah, all steep) and then the sources of difference (rock, aspect, shelter)
slides.1.content: How to write a comparison: same variety, different rock and aspect → one set of axes → a one-line conclusion such as 'Côte-Rôtie leans aromatic, Hermitage leans structural'.
slides.2.title: North vs south vs Australia: Syrah in different climates
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Northern Rhône Syrah (semi-continental)
slides.2.highlights.0.content: General account: black pepper, violets, blackberry, smoke and bacon fat; medium to high acidity, marked tannin, medium to high alcohol
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Southern Rhône Syrah (Mediterranean)
slides.2.highlights.1.content: General account: riper, rounder fruit with plum, spice and garrigue; often the colour and frame partner to Grenache rather than the lead
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Australian Shiraz
slides.2.highlights.2.content: General account: warmth and sunshine bring ripe black fruit, sweet spice and higher alcohol; styles range from full-bodied Barossa to peppery cool-climate examples, so name the region rather than just 'Australia'
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Blind-tasting cues
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Pepper + violets + smoke + medium to high acid → leans northern Rhône; ripe black fruit + sweet spice + low acid + high alcohol → leans warm regions (southern Rhône or Australia), then use oak style and wider New/Old World cues to separate them
slides.2.content: Syrah and Shiraz are the same variety: the difference comes from climate, picking time and winemaking, not the grape.
slides.3.title: Southern Rhône: Châteauneuf-du-Pape vs Gigondas vs Vacqueyras
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Strict specification (hand harvest and sorting, 35 hl/ha, minimum 12.5%); multi-variety blends; pebbly soils. General account: full-bodied, high alcohol, ripe red and black fruit and herbs, with a wide stylistic range from modern to traditional
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Gigondas
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Grenache ≥50%, with Cinsault + Mourvèdre + Syrah together ≥15% (INAO). General account: foothill vineyards, more structure and tannin, often compared with Châteauneuf but more rustic and more affordable
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Vacqueyras
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Grenache ≥50% and Syrah + Mourvèdre ≥20% (INAO). General account: a larger role for Syrah, with more open fruit and spice; both red and white are made
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Comparison framework
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Put rules (proportions, yields), soil, altitude and style in one table; in essays note that proportion rules are similar and style differences come from site and estate, and do not confuse legal numbers with style impressions
slides.3.content: The point of comparing southern crus is a shared Grenache base with different sites and house styles; do not conclude from one or two adjectives.
slides.4.title: A contrast with Burgundy's Pinot Noir
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Variety character
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Syrah: deep colour, marked tannin, black fruit and pepper; Pinot Noir: thin skins, paler colour, fine tannin, red berries, earthiness and higher acidity. Both express place clearly, in different ways (general account)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Classification logic
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Burgundy classifies by plot (climat): Bourgogne → village → Premier Cru → Grand Cru; the Rhône classifies by appellation: Côtes du Rhône → Villages → independent crus (one cru = one AOC, a whole village or hill). The key difference: Burgundy ranks sites within a village, Rhône crus do not subdivide into ranked vineyards
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Single variety vs blend
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Red Burgundy centres on Pinot Noir; the northern Rhône also centres on Syrah (Cornas 100%), but southern crus are blends by default (13 varieties in Châteauneuf). Good material for 'terroir expression vs blend composition' essays
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Link to existing courses
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Compare with the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune lessons of the Burgundy course: put Côte-Rôtie / Hermitage rock and aspect beside the Côte d'Or limestone slope and exposure in one table. This lesson does not repeat Burgundy content, it only supplies the axes
slides.4.content: A high-scoring essay explains why different classification logics reflect different histories and markets, not just a list of differences.
slides.5.title: Variety profiles: descriptors for Diploma tasting
slides.5.highlights.0.title: Grenache
slides.5.highlights.0.content: Pale to medium ruby, red cherry and strawberry, sweet spice; high alcohol, low to medium tannin, medium acidity; garnet rims and early oxidative development are common (general account)
slides.5.highlights.1.title: Mourvèdre
slides.5.highlights.1.content: Deep colour, firm tannin, meaty, black fruit and leather; late-ripening and needs warmth to ripen (general account)
slides.5.highlights.2.title: Viognier
slides.5.highlights.2.content: Peach, apricot, white flowers, honeysuckle; low acid, high alcohol, full body; dull if under-ripe and oily if over-ripe (general account)
slides.5.highlights.3.title: Marsanne and Roussanne
slides.5.highlights.3.content: Marsanne: waxy, almond, round, low to medium acid; Roussanne: herbal tea, pear, higher acidity and tension, longer-lived (general account)
slides.5.highlights.4.title: Cinsault and Carignan
slides.5.highlights.4.content: Cinsault: light, red fruit, good for rosé and blends; Carignan: concentrated from old vines, high in acid and tannin (general account)
slides.5.content: Write each variety profile in three parts, colour / aroma / structure, then add the region and style it points to.
slides.6.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What is the key difference between Rhône cru classification and Burgundy's?
A. Rhône ranks by plot (climat), Burgundy by appellation name
B. Burgundy ranks sites within a village (Premier / Grand Cru) while a Rhône cru is an independent AOC with no ranked vineyards inside
C. They are identical
D. The Rhône has no classification
One Rhône cru = one AOC, whereas Burgundy ranks plots below village level.
Which description most likely points to northern Rhône Syrah?
A. Pepper, violets, smoke, medium to high acidity
B. Strawberry, low tannin, very pale colour
C. Tropical fruit and honey, low acid
D. Caramel, nuts, oxidation
Pepper, violets, smoke and higher acidity are classic cues for northern Rhône Syrah (general account).
What is the Gigondas red specification?
A. Grenache ≥50%, with Cinsault + Mourvèdre + Syrah together ≥15%
B. Syrah ≥80%
C. 100% Grenache
D. Mourvèdre ≥50%
Gigondas: Grenache ≥50% and Cinsault + Mourvèdre + Syrah ≥15% (INAO).
How are Syrah and Shiraz related?
A. Two different varieties
B. The same variety; style differences come mainly from climate, picking time and winemaking
C. Shiraz always uses oak chips
D. Syrah can only be grown in France
Syrah and Shiraz are the same grape; the name often hints at style, but the differences come from site and winemaking.
